title: Entailment-Checklist Scoring: An API-Free Alternative to LLM-Based Dense Video Caption Evaluation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to characterize why existing API-free metrics fail for checklist-based dense video caption evaluation. None of the prior papers explicitly address this purpose. Papers [6], [10], [15], and [16] discuss evaluation metrics for image captioning, but they do not analyze failures of API-free metrics in the context of checklist-based dense video captioning. Similarly, papers [7], [8], [14], [23], and [24] explore LLM-based evaluation methods but do not focus on the failure modes of API-free metrics for dense video captioning. No prior paper establishes the same empirical relationship or addresses this specific gap.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves correlating BERTScore and embedding-based similarity metrics against LLM (Gemini) judgments on checklist keypoint coverage and inspecting induced system rankings. Paper [11] introduces BERTScore as a metric for text generation evaluation, and paper [12] discusses embedding-based similarity metrics. Both papers cover the underlying primitives of the mechanism (correlation of metrics with judgments and embedding-based similarity). While the application to dense video captioning is new, the mechanism itself is not novel.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring Spearman correlations between metrics (BERTScore and embedding-based methods) and LLM judgments, as well as inspecting system rankings. Paper [11] evaluates BERTScore using correlation with human judgments, and paper [12] evaluates embedding-based metrics using rank-based similarity. Paper [14] also evaluates LLM judge scores using correlation and ranking analysis. These prior works cover the evaluation design, even though the specific objects (e.g., dense video captions) differ.

### Domain
The domain is dense video captioning evaluation. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], and [9] all address dense video captioning, covering this domain. While the specific focus on checklist-based evaluation is new, the general application area of dense video captioning is well-covered.

The mechanism, **Entailment-Checklist Scoring (ECS)**, involves a two-stage retrieve-then-verify pipeline: (1) retrieving candidate caption sentences using embedding similarity and (2) verifying keypoint entailment with an open NLI model. This mechanism is **covered** by prior work. Specifically, [9] formulates relation classification as textual entailment and demonstrates the use of textual entailment models for verifying relationships, which aligns with the second stage of ECS.
